title: The righteous shall live by faith (Romans 1:17)
hook: a tormented monk named Luther reads Romans and feels the gates of paradise open

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word indulgence: a gift that became a price, and voices across the church asking for reform. Your line was always reforming.

A friar kneels in confession, and he's been there a long time. He lists his sins, remembers more, and goes back. He fasts, prays through the night, follows the rule of his order to the letter, and still can't shake the feeling that God is a judge waiting to condemn him. His name is Martin Luther, a monk who teaches the Bible at the university in Wittenberg. Looking back years later, he wrote that one phrase in Paul's letter to the Romans had become hateful to him.

Here's the verse, in the King James Bible, Romans chapter one: "For therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith: as it is written, The just shall live by faith." As it is written: Paul is quoting the prophet Habakkuk, who says, "the just shall live by his faith." The phrase Luther hated was the righteousness of God. He'd been taught to hear it, he says, as God's own justice, the righteousness by which God punishes the unrighteous. And if that's what the gospel reveals, how is it good news? So he kept beating at the verse, his word, until he saw it differently. The righteousness of God here, he came to think, isn't what God demands of people but what God gives them: a gift, received by trusting it. In his own telling, he felt born again, as if he'd walked through open gates into paradise itself, and the whole Bible looked different afterward. Christians still disagree about how faith and good works fit together. Lutherans and other Protestants stress that people are made right with God by grace through faith, as a gift. Catholic and Orthodox teaching also says it is all grace, and speaks of faith working through love, growing over a lifetime. Today, Catholic and Lutheran churches have signed a joint statement saying they share a basic understanding here, while still differing in emphasis. But the moment in the study belongs to Luther: a frightened man, a single verse, and gates he hadn't known were open.

Say the verse in your head, the just shall live by faith; then again, leaning on just; again, leaning on live; and then only the last two words, by faith. Notice which word you lean on, and whether it sounds like a demand or a gift today; there's no right answer. If you pray, let the line become a prayer as it is; if you don't, just let it sit.
Habakkuk. The prophet Paul quotes in Romans: the just shall live by faith, the verse Luther first heard as a threat and then as a gift.
Your line: the gates opened. Some things can only be received, never earned. Day eight hundred fifty-two, done.

howItsDone: Justification by faith is a central theme of Lutheran teaching, and Christians across traditions study Romans together, often reading Paul alongside the prophet he quotes.

chat.says: What changed for Luther when he reread Romans one seventeen?
options: He came to read God's righteousness as a gift received by trust, not a demand to earn.
He decided Paul had made the phrase up, so he stopped trusting the Old Testament.
He concluded that God's justice only punishes, so he gave up on good news.
chat.meaning: Luther had heard the righteousness of God as punishing justice. Rereading Paul quoting Habakkuk, he saw it as God's gift, received by faith.

Habakkuk.meaning: a Hebrew prophet whom Paul quotes in Romans

righteousness.meaning: being right or just; Luther first heard it as punishing justice

notes: Claims rule: no dates stated. The word field keeps the index's truncated head ('The righteous shall live by faith') exactly as the outline requires; the spoken word segment uses the full phrase. Owner may want the index word fixed.
The KJV of Romans 1:17 reads 'The just shall live by faith', not 'the righteous'; the title is the outline's. The teach quotes the KJV.

Luther's account (his 1545 preface) paraphrased: he hated the phrase 'the righteousness of God', understood as active/punishing justice; he 'beat importunately' on Paul; he felt 'altogether born again' and 'entered paradise itself through open gates'. 'Looking back years later' and 'written late in life' are drawn from the preface's retrospective framing. Confirm.

Hook details (long confessions, fasting, vigils) are from Luther's later recollections and his confessor Staupitz's reported impatience; confirm phrasing. 'A small university in Wittenberg' is general history.
Catholic and Orthodox views summarized briefly ('all grace', 'faith working through love', growing over a lifetime); Orthodox scholars may prefer 'theosis' language. Confirm both summaries are fair.
Joint Declaration (1999) referenced without date as 'in our own time'; confirm.

Editor pass: practice rewritten so the spoken emphasis is audible (the repeated identical lines could not be heard as different); 'small university' and the trapdoor's 'written late in life' (unsourced age claim) cut; howItsDone's claim that Romans 1:17 is often read on Reformation Sunday removed (the usual lectionary reading is Romans 3).

Second editor: review no longer says the church was 'full of people' asking for reform (day 851 softened that to voices across the church); 'Catholics and Orthodox Christians also teach' narrowed to their churches' teaching; 'young' cut from the hook.

Auditor (day 847-856 pass): garbled agreement fixed ('teaching also says ... and speak' to 'says ... and speaks'). Romans 1:17 and Habakkuk 2:4 match the KJV. Note the Joint Declaration is Catholic-Lutheran; the Orthodox were not signatories, and the script does not say they were.
